title: Short sets, encores and the audience
summary: Greene says the men would like to stretch out and that audiences are mostly over fifty.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Freddie, listen, does it ever -- I mean the fact that the gigs now -- they're all involved with a 45 minute performance, and an intermission, and then another 45 minute performance -- which is absolutely nothing like what it once was to play in a band. And, you know, your repertoire is limited and everything -- do you think anybody minds anymore or do you think everybody's just so content to not work too hard, and too long, and get your money just the same, or do you think there's ever times when the guys themselves would like to stretch out?
I think so.
You do?
I do. I think the guys would like to stretch out a little more, because, you know, some of the guys usually go to jam sessions, like, afterwards, if they can find a place to go.
They still do?
Yeah. If they can find a place to go.
But, they can't find them too easily?
Yeah. It's hard to find a place. You can't find it like years ago, you know?
I mean, it's a shame, because, I mean that's the thing about a band, as you said to us before. I mean, you're playing, and, I mean, in the days when people played dances, and you played a set,

it might have been very nice and fine. But, then you play the next set, and for no reason everything is jumping. Everything's terrific, and everybody's really enjoying it. And, if you don't have about seven or eight sets to play a night, or six or something, this can't happen. You've just got two set sets. And, you can't expect anything to happen except what you -- what's supposed to happen.
Yeah. Right. Well, it's a contract thing, you know. That's what I's called. But, we usually play encores, you see?
Yeah. That's right.

We've been doing that quite a bit. Like, we play our regular time, and the public wants more, and so we give them more, you know. We play another number, or -- and if they're not pleased, you know -- if they want more, we give them another number, and then we play the theme song. We usually add two numbers, you know, to the regular format.
Yeah.

When you played this concert you had in Sarasota, now that went -- the playing time must have been over two hours. And, as Helen said, no singer. And, not a very long drum solo. And, everybody in that band got to be featured, you know. It was a very good concert.
Mm hmm.
It was a very nice concert.
Oh, yeah?
And, the audience down there -- the average age was over fifty, but they ate it up.
Oh, yeah. Well, we've been doing that quite a bit. You know, like, our audiences, like, as a rule are like, over fifty, but I've noticed there's alot of kids. Alot of kids are really, you know --
Well, it isn't that it's a young looking band.
Mm hmm. That's what I'm saying, you know what I mean? And, it really make us feel good, you know, that these kids, you know -- coming around, you know?
Yeah. So they're hearing what's you're laying down.
Yeah. They're hearing what's -- right. Because it's all new to them, you know. And, it's really a great thing to --.
Especially for them to hear blues and things that they really don't get to hear anywhere else, do they?
Right. Right. I know. No.
But, it's served up with a -- Basie serves it up with a flair and everything, so that the kids can dig on it.
Yeah.
